name: Urban St. Louis
blurb: Oaks, squirrels, city coyotes and falcons in Forest Park and the neighborhoods.

tip.title: Remove the city coyote
tip.text: Coyotes are the top predator on the ground in St. Louis parks. Set Coyote to -100% and watch rabbits, deer and raccoons.

notes: Feeding links were checked against the sources listed where they state them. Where the sources are silent, links come from general ecological knowledge and are illustrative. Feeding links that match a GloBI (Global Biotic Interactions) record are marked in the node details, with a link to the records. A few links were added from GloBI records.

nodes.name: Street & park oaks
nodes.desc: Large shade trees of St. Louis parks and streets. Their acorns feed squirrels and deer, and their leaves host many caterpillars.

nodes.name: Lawns & park turf
nodes.desc: Mown grass that covers much of the city's parks and yards. It feeds rabbits and a large community of insects.
An omnivore that eats acorns, nuts, buds and fruit, and raids bird feeders and trash bins near people. Hawks are among its main predators.
Browses garden plants, young growth and acorns in larger parks and greenbelts. Coyotes are among the predators of fawns.
Grazes lawns and garden plants. Cottontails are prey for hawks and coyotes.
Eats earthworms and insects plus a lot of fruit and berries. Accipiter hawks are among its main predators.
A seed-eating bird closely tied to buildings and people, also taking scraps and insects. A common prey of Cooper's hawks.
An adaptable omnivore. Wikipedia describes it eating invertebrates, plants and small vertebrates, using garbage in cities, and dabbling for fish and crayfish at the water's edge.
An introduced omnivore that forages on lawns for insects and also takes scraps. It is common prey for urban hawks and falcons.
A large hawk that hunts squirrels, rabbits and other small mammals around parks and highways.
Lives in the city. Wikipedia says urban coyotes eat rabbits, rodents, birds, fruit and trash, and that small pets (especially cats) can be taken.
Nests on tall buildings and bridges. In cities its diet is dominated by pigeons, with starlings, robins and swifts also taken.
Powers growth of trees, lawns and gardens.
Spring and summer rain waters the city's trees and lawns, supplemented by irrigation.

nodes.name: Fungi, worms & bacteria
nodes.desc: Break down fallen leaves and dead animals and return nutrients to the soil.

story: Urban St. Louis is located in Missouri, USA, with coordinates 38.63, -90.25. It is home to Forest Park, a public park in western St. Louis covering 1,326 acres that opened in 1876. The park features meadows, trees, ponds, lakes, and freshwater streams, and has restored prairie and wetlands areas that attract a greater variety of birds and wildlife.
matters: The park's restored natural habitats reduce flooding and attract an increased variety of birds and wildlife. These habitats provide homes for many species, including urban coyotes, peregrine falcons, Cooper's hawks, and raccoons.
